## Solution

Let $d = \gcd(x,y)$, $a = x/d$, $b = y/d$, so $\gcd(a,b)=1$. Since $d\mid x$ and $d\mid y$, vertices in different residue classes mod $d$ are never adjacent. The graph decomposes into $d$ components, each isomorphic to a distance graph on a path with distances $\{a,b\}$. So $\chi(G)$ equals the chromatic number of the distance graph on $\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ with distances $\{a,b\}$, for $M \approx n^2/d$.

Since $\gcd(a,b)=1$, at most one of $a,b$ is even. There are two cases.

### Case 1: Both $a$ and $b$ are odd (equivalently $v_2(x)=v_2(y)$)

**Upper bound ($\chi \le 2$):** Color vertex $k$ (in each relabeled component) by $k \bmod 2$. Since $a$ and $b$ are both odd, vertices at distance $a$ or $b$ have different parities. This is a valid 2-coloring.

**Lower bound ($\chi \ge 2$):** The graph has edges (since $n\ge 2$ ensures at least one pair at distance $x$ or $y$).

So $\chi = 2$.

### Case 2: One of $a,b$ is even, the other odd (equivalently $v_2(x)\ne v_2(y)$)

WLOG $a$ even, $b$ odd.

**Upper bound ($\chi \le 3$):** Set $p = a+b$, which is odd. Since $b \equiv -a \pmod{p}$, the circulant graph $C_p(a,b) = C_p(a) \cup C_p(-a) = C_p(a)$. Because $\gcd(a,p)=\gcd(a,a+b)=\gcd(a,b)=1$, we have $C_p(a) \cong C_p$ (the cycle on $p$ vertices). Since $p\ge 3$ is odd, $\chi(C_p)=3$. Take any proper 3-coloring $\varphi$ of $C_p$ and extend periodically: $c(k)=\varphi(k\bmod p)$. For any $i,j$ with $|i-j|\in\{a,b\}$, we have $i-j \equiv \pm a \pmod{p}$, so $c(i)\ne c(j)$. Scaling back to distances $x=da, y=db$ gives a proper 3-coloring of $G$.

**Lower bound ($\chi \ge 3$):** We exhibit an odd cycle. In component $G_1$ (relabeled as positions $0,1,2,\ldots$), consider the closed walk:
$$0,\; a,\; 2a,\; \ldots,\; ba,\; ba-b,\; ba-2b,\; \ldots,\; ba-(a{-}1)b = b,\; 0.$$
This uses $b$ steps of size $a$ and $a$ steps of size $b$, totaling $a+b$ steps. Since $a$ is even and $b$ is odd, $a+b$ is **odd**.

**Distinctness:** The first part gives vertices $\{ja : 0\le j\le b\}$; the second gives $\{ba-kb : 1\le k\le a{-}1\} = \{mb : 1\le m\le a{-}1\}$. If $ja = mb$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$, then $a\mid m$, but $1\le m\le a-1$ makes this impossible. So all $a+b$ vertices are distinct, forming an odd cycle.

**Fits within $n^2$ cells:** The maximum position is $ab$, corresponding to cell $1+abd = 1+xy/d$. Since $x\ne y$ and $x,y\le n$:
- If $d=1$: at least one of $x,y$ is $\le n-1$, so $xy \le n(n-1) < n^2$, giving $1+xy/d \le n^2$.
- If $d\ge 2$: $xy/d \le n^2/2 < n^2$ (and $d\ge 2$ forces $n\ge 3$), so $1+xy/d \le n^2$.

The odd cycle fits, so $G$ is not bipartite, hence $\chi \ge 3$.

Combining: $\chi = 3$.

### Conclusion

The minimum number of colors is:

$$\boxed{\begin{cases} 2 & \text{if } v_2(x) = v_2(y) \text{ (i.e., } x/\gcd(x,y) \text{ and } y/\gcd(x,y) \text{ are both odd)}, \\ 3 & \text{if } v_2(x) \ne v_2(y) \text{ (i.e., one of } x/\gcd(x,y),\, y/\gcd(x,y) \text{ is even)}. \end{cases}}$$
